chunks: Herein 'mirward' is a form derived from 'irwād' which means to allow time, to wait for. It is an extremely eloquent and wonderful expression. It is as though Amīr al-mu’minīn, peace be upon him, has likened the period of Banū Umayyah to a limited area meant for the training of horses for racing where they are running towards the limit, so that when they reach its extremity their organization will be destroyed.

key_terms.الْإِرْوَادِ: The root concept of allowing time or waiting.
key_terms.الْمُضْمَارِ: The racetrack or training ground for horses.
key_terms.الْمُهْلَةَ: The period of respite or delay.
key_terms.انْقَضَّ نِظَامُهُمْ: Their system/organization was destroyed or collapsed.
key_terms.وَالْمِرْوَدُ: The term 'mirward', referring to a period of delay or waiting.

ai.seo_question: What is the meaning of 'mirward' in the context of Umayyad rule in Nahj al-Balagha?
ai.summary: Sharif al-Radi interprets 'mirward' as a period of delay and manifestation, employing the metaphor of a racetrack (mudmar) to illustrate the transient nature of Umayyad power. He suggests that just as horses lose their momentum upon reaching the end of the track, the Umayyad system will inevitably collapse once its allotted time expires, highlighting the divine wisdom behind their temporary rule.
